lessons.title: Social Insects: Termites and Bees
lessons.objective: Differentiate the castes of termites and bees and explain how division of labour helps the colony.

content.heading: Social insects
paragraphs: A termite mound and a beehive look like crowded chaos, but both are organised societies. A few individuals reproduce, while thousands of sterile workers keep the colony fed, defended and clean.

content.heading: Termite castes
paragraphs: Termites are social insects with a queen, king, workers, soldiers and alates. The queen has a swollen abdomen and lays eggs. The king stays beside her, unlike the male bee. Workers are blind, pale and soft-bodied. They build galleries, forage, feed the queen and young, and some tend fungus gardens.

Soldiers have large heads and strong mandibles, and some squirt defensive fluid from a frontal gland. Alates are winged reproductives that swarm after rain, shed their wings and start new colonies. Sterile workers, overlapping generations and cooperative brood care make the colony eusocial.
bullets: The queen lays eggs and the king stays with her.
Workers build, forage and feed the colony.
Soldiers defend, while alates disperse and reproduce.
content.takeaway: Termite castes divide reproduction, work and defence.

check.question: Which termite caste has large mandibles and defends the colony?
check.why: Soldiers have enlarged heads and mandibles, and some also squirt defensive fluid.

content.heading: Bee castes
paragraphs: A honeybee colony has one queen, thousands of sterile female workers and a few hundred male drones. The queen lays eggs and produces pheromones that suppress worker reproduction and keep the colony together. Workers are female. Their jobs change with age: cleaning, nursing, comb building, guarding and foraging. They have pollen baskets, wax glands and a sting.

Drones are male. They fertilise a new queen on a mating flight and die after mating. They have no sting and are expelled before a period of food shortage. Only females have stings, because the sting is a modified ovipositor.
bullets: One queen, many sterile female workers and a few male drones.
Worker jobs change with age.
Drones mate once and die; workers defend the hive.
content.takeaway: Bee castes divide reproduction, housework and mating.

check.question: Which bee is male and fertilises the queen?
check.why: Drones are the male bees; they mate with a new queen and die afterwards.

content.heading: Division of labour and communication
paragraphs: Social life works because workers share genes with the queen's offspring, so helping the colony can pass on those shared genes. Division of labour also raises efficiency: each caste specialises in one job instead of every individual doing everything.

Pheromones coordinate the colony. The queen pheromone suppresses worker reproduction, alarm pheromones mobilise defenders, and trail pheromones guide termites to food. The bee waggle dance tells other workers the direction and distance of a food source. Termites develop gradually through nymphs, while bees pass through egg, larva, pupa and adult. Termites recycle wood and return nutrients to the soil, but they also damage timber and buildings. Bees pollinate crops and produce honey and wax.
bullets: Division of labour raises colony efficiency.
Pheromones coordinate work, alarm and food trails.
Termites recycle wood; bees pollinate and make honey.
content.takeaway: A social insect colony is a division of labour held together by chemical signals.

check.question: The bee waggle dance communicates
options: The direction and distance of food
check.why: The dance encodes the direction and distance of a food source.

visual.caption: Two societies, two ways to divide the work.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Termites have a king; bees do not. Soldiers are termites; guard workers are bees. Termites are not ants, even though both live in colonies.

lessons.title: Feeding Adaptations
lessons.objective: Relate bird beaks and feet, and insect mouthparts, to the food each organism eats.

content.heading: Feeding adaptations
paragraphs: A hawk's beak tears meat, a sunbird's beak probes a flower, and a mosquito's mouthparts pierce skin. Feeding structures are shaped by diet, and the exam asks you to match the structure to the food.

content.heading: Bird beaks
paragraphs: A bird's beak is its main feeding tool, and its shape follows the diet. Insectivorous birds have slender, pointed beaks for picking insects; the woodpecker uses a chisel beak and a long tongue to extract grubs. Granivorous birds have short, stout, conical beaks for cracking seeds. Nectar-feeding birds have long, slender, curved beaks for probing flowers.

Carnivorous birds have strong, hooked beaks for tearing flesh. Ducks have broad, flat beaks with lamellae for filtering food from water. Vultures have hooked beaks for tearing carrion. Beaks are also used for preening, nest building and defence, so a single shape can serve more than one job.
bullets: Beak shape follows diet.
Hooked beaks tear, conical beaks crack and long beaks probe.
A woodpecker uses a chisel beak and a long tongue.
content.takeaway: Read the diet from the shape of the beak.

check.question: A short, stout, conical beak is best suited for
check.why: A short, stout, conical beak can crack hard seed coats.

content.heading: Bird legs and feet
paragraphs: Bird feet are adapted to habitat and hunting method. Perching birds have three toes forward and one back, which grip a branch. Raptors have strong talons for seizing prey. Wading birds have long legs and spread toes for walking in shallow water. Swimming birds have webbed feet that push against water.

Running birds have long, strong legs and reduced toes. Climbing birds, such as woodpeckers and parrots, have two toes forward and two back, a grip that holds bark or branches. The same foot can be used for walking, scratching, defence and carrying food, so the structure reflects the bird's whole way of life.
bullets: Webbed feet swim; long legs wade.
Talons seize prey; perching feet grip branches.
Leg structure matches habitat and hunting method.
content.takeaway: Feet show where a bird lives and how it catches food.

check.question: A duck's webbed feet are an adaptation for
check.why: Webbed feet paddle efficiently through water.

content.heading: Insect mouthparts
paragraphs: Insect mouthparts are matched to food and feeding method. Biting-chewing insects, such as grasshoppers, cockroaches and beetles, have hard mandibles for cutting solid food. Piercing-sucking insects, such as the female mosquito, aphid and tsetse fly, have needle-like stylets that pierce and suck.

Siphoning insects, such as butterflies and moths, have a long coiled proboscis for nectar. Houseflies have sponging mouthparts that absorb liquids. Bees have chewing-lapping mouthparts for nectar and pollen. The male mosquito feeds on nectar; only the female bites, because she needs blood for her eggs. Mouthpart type is one of the most reliable clues to an insect's diet.
bullets: Mosquito: piercing-sucking; butterfly: siphoning.
Housefly: sponging; bee: chewing-lapping.
Only the female mosquito takes blood.
content.takeaway: Insect mouthparts are tools matched to the food and feeding method.

check.why: A long coiled proboscis that siphons nectar is the siphoning type.

visual.caption: Solid food is cut; liquid food is pierced and sucked.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The female mosquito bites; the male feeds on nectar. A butterfly's proboscis is coiled at rest and extended to feed. Read the sex and the food before choosing a mouthpart.

lessons.title: Defence and Mating Adaptations
lessons.objective: Explain how structures and behaviour protect organisms from predators and help them secure mates.

content.heading: Defence and mating adaptations
paragraphs: A stick insect freezes like a twig, a praying mantis raises spiny forelegs, a toad inflates its body, and a male Agama flashes its red head. Defence and mating are both contests, and adaptations are the weapons.

content.heading: Defence: hide, startle, fight
paragraphs: Camouflage is the first defence. A stick insect resembles a twig and a praying mantis resembles a leaf, so a predator may pass without noticing them. If detected, a startle display can frighten an attacker: the praying mantis raises its spiny forelegs and wings, and the eyed hawk-moth exposes eyespots.

Physical barriers raise the cost of attack. Hedgehogs and porcupines have spines, snails have shells, and some caterpillars have irritating hairs. Chemical defence is common: toads secrete toxins from parotoid glands, millipedes release irritating fluids, and stink bugs spray a foul smell. A toad can also inflate its body to look larger, and a lizard can drop its tail to escape.
bullets: Camouflage avoids detection; startle displays frighten.
Spines, shells and toxins raise the cost of attack.
Autotomy and fleeing remove the animal from danger.
content.takeaway: Defence works by hiding, startling, blocking or poisoning the attacker.

check.question: A toad's parotoid glands are an adaptation for
check.why: The glands secrete toxins that deter predators, which is chemical defence.

content.heading: Mating: signal, compete, display
paragraphs: Sexual dimorphism means males and females differ in size, colour or structure. In Agama lizards, the dominant male has a bright red or orange head and a blue body, while the female is duller. The male displays and defends a territory, and the colour advertises his condition to females and rivals. A territory secures food, shelter and mates, and reduces fighting.

Birds use displays: a peacock fans his tail, a male weaver builds and displays a nest, and some males feed their partners during courtship. Males also compete directly. Deer use antlers, goats use horns, and baboons fight for dominance, though most contests are ritualised rather than fatal. Bright colours and large weapons carry costs: they attract predators and use energy.
bullets: Sexual dimorphism separates male and female appearance.
Display and territory advertise quality.
Bright colours and weapons carry survival costs.
content.takeaway: Mating adaptations advertise or defend access to a mate.

check.question: The bright red head of a male Agama lizard is mainly for
check.why: The red head is a sexual signal used in display and territory defence.

content.heading: Balancing defence and display
paragraphs: The same structure can serve defence and display. Antlers and horns are used in combat and also advertise strength. Bright colours attract mates but make a male easier for a predator to see. A chameleon changes colour for camouflage, temperature control and communication, so one skin serves several jobs.

Parental care extends defence to offspring. Cichlid fish guard their eggs, birds mob predators near the nest, and mammals defend their young. The balance is never perfect: survival and reproduction pull in different directions, and each adaptation is a compromise that raises fitness in its own habitat.
bullets: One structure can serve defence and display.
Sexual signals trade safety for mating success.
Parental care is defence extended to offspring.
content.takeaway: Survival and reproduction pull in opposite directions, and adaptations balance them.

check.why: The tail is a courtship display; its cost is carried because it improves mating success.

visual.caption: Survival and reproduction pull in different directions.

content.body: Agama males are the red-headed sex; females are duller. Bright male colour is sexual selection, not warning colouration. Not every horn is a defence structure.

lessons.title: Temperature and Water Regulation
lessons.objective: Explain how organisms regulate body temperature and conserve water, using basking, hibernation, aestivation, skin coverings, spines and scales.

content.heading: Temperature and water regulation
paragraphs: A lizard basks on a rock, a frog buries itself in mud, a cactus has spines, and a camel has thick fur. Each solves the same two problems: keeping the body at a workable temperature and holding on to water.

content.heading: Temperature regulation
paragraphs: Endotherms, such as birds and mammals, generate heat internally and keep a fairly constant body temperature. Hair, fur, feathers and blubber insulate. Sweating and vasodilation lose heat through the skin, panting loses heat through the mouth and lungs, and shivering and vasoconstriction conserve it. Ectotherms, such as lizards, amphibians and fish, gain heat from the environment, so their body temperature varies.

A lizard basks by flattening its body and turning broadside to the sun, then retreats to shade when it is too hot. Hibernation is winter dormancy, with low metabolism and stored fat. Aestivation is summer drought dormancy, used by lungfish and some snails. The two look similar, but the season and the trigger are different.
bullets: Endotherms generate heat; ectotherms gain it from the environment.
Basking, shade and burrowing control temperature behaviourally.
Hibernation is winter; aestivation is summer drought.
content.takeaway: Temperature control is either internal heat production or behaviour in the habitat.

check.question: A lizard lying on a rock in the morning is
check.why: The lizard gains heat from the sun and the warm rock, which is basking.

content.heading: Water conservation in animals
paragraphs: Desert animals reduce water loss in several ways. Thick fur or scales limit evaporation, the kidneys produce concentrated urine, the faeces are dry, and sweat glands are few. Many are nocturnal or burrow during the day. The camel stores fat in its hump as an energy reserve, while its kidneys and nose reduce water loss.

Reptile scales are waterproof keratin, and pangolin scales, the only mammalian scales, are keratin too; both reduce water loss and add protection. Insects have a waxy cuticle, spiracles that can close, and Malpighian tubules that concentrate waste. Freshwater fish excrete dilute urine, while marine fish drink water and excrete excess salts. Each strategy keeps the body's water and salt balance within limits.
bullets: Waterproof coverings reduce evaporation.
Concentrated urine and dry faeces conserve water.
Nocturnal and burrowing behaviour avoids heat.
content.takeaway: Water conservation means reducing loss and concentrating waste.

check.question: Which feature helps a desert mammal conserve water?
check.why: Concentrated urine removes waste with less water loss.

content.heading: Water conservation in plants
paragraphs: Xerophytes are plants adapted to dry habitats. They have a thick cuticle, sunken stomata, rolled or hairy leaves, and reduced leaf area. Some have deep roots, others have shallow widespread roots, and succulents store water in thick stems or leaves. CAM photosynthesis lets them open stomata at night, when water loss is lower.

Cactus spines are modified leaves. They reduce surface area and transpiration, and they deter herbivores. Hydrophytes, such as water lilies, have large air spaces, a thin cuticle, stomata on the upper surface and poorly developed roots. Mesophytes, including most Nigerian crops, sit between the two extremes.
bullets: Xerophytes reduce water loss with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata.
Spines are modified leaves that cut transpiration.
Hydrophytes have air spaces and little waterproofing.
content.takeaway: A plant's water strategy shows in its leaves, stomata and roots.

lessons.title: Root and Stem Anatomy
lessons.objective: Identify transverse sections of a root and a stem and relate their structure to their functions.

content.heading: Root and stem
paragraphs: A transverse section through a root or stem is a map you can read. From the outside in, each ring has a job, and the jobs follow the plant's two supply routes.

content.heading: The root slice
paragraphs: In a transverse section of a dicot root, the layers run outside to inside: epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, ending at the vascular cylinder.

The epidermis covers the root and bears root hairs, which take up water and dissolved mineral salts. The cortex stores starch and moves water inwards. The endodermis's Casparian strip is a waxy band that blocks the spaces between cells, so water and salts must cross its cell membranes before reaching the xylem. The pericycle, just inside the endodermis, gives rise to branch roots.
The vascular cylinder carries the xylem as a solid star in a dicot root, with phloem patches between the arms. In a monocot root, the centre is a large pith instead, and the xylem has many arms.
bullets: Epidermis with root hairs: absorbs water and salts.
Endodermis with Casparian strip: the checkpoint into the xylem.
Xylem star in dicots; pith centre in monocots.
content.takeaway: The root slice works from outside in: hair, membrane, xylem.

check.question: The Casparian strip is found in the cells of the
check.why: The Casparian strip blocks spaces between cells in the endodermis.

content.heading: The stem slice
paragraphs: In a transverse section of a dicot stem, the layers run outside to inside: cuticle and epidermis, cortex, vascular bundles arranged in a ring and a large pith at the centre.

Each vascular bundle has xylem on the inside, towards the pith, and phloem on the outside, with cambium between them. The cambium is meristematic and produces the thickening layer of wood in woody plants. In a monocot stem, the bundles are scattered through the ground tissue, there is no cambium, and secondary growth is absent.
The pith in a dicot stem stores starch and some nutrients; in monocots a distinct pith is usually not obvious because of the scattered bundles.
bullets: Epidermis and cuticle reduce water loss.
Xylem inside, phloem outside, cambium between.
Scattered bundles and no cambium: monocot stem.
content.takeaway: Ring plus cambium means wood; scattered bundles mean not.

check.question: In a dicot stem T.S., the xylem of a vascular bundle lies
check.why: Each dicot vascular bundle points its xylem inwards, towards the pith.

content.heading: Structure matched to function
paragraphs: Root hairs multiply the absorption surface; the waxy cuticle reduces evaporation; air spaces in the cortex supply the deeper cells. Xylem runs from root to leaf, moving water up; phloem runs from leaf to root, moving food down.

Lignified xylem and the sclerenchyma fibres supporting the vascular bundles give stems their rigidity. Where a stem is still young and tender, collenchyma under the epidermis bends instead of breaking. Roots anchor the plant, and their branch roots emerge from the pericycle.

When you see a section, match the arrangement to its organ: star-shaped xylem with no pith is a dicot root; a large pith centre is a monocot root; bundles in a ring with cambium is a dicot stem; scattered bundles is a monocot stem.
bullets: Root hairs increase the absorbing surface.
Xylem goes up; phloem goes down.
Ring plus cambium is dicot; scattered is monocot.
content.takeaway: A section is a map: read the arrangement and you name the organ.

lessons.title: Leaf Anatomy
lessons.objective: Identify a transverse section of a leaf and relate leaf structure to photosynthesis and gas exchange.

content.heading: Leaf anatomy
paragraphs: A leaf is a solar panel and a gas-exchange surface in one. Its transverse section shows exactly how light and air reach the chloroplasts.

content.heading: The upper surface
paragraphs: From outside in, the upper surface is a waxy cuticle, then the upper epidermis. The cuticle is a waterproof layer that limits uncontrolled evaporation, and the upper epidermis is usually transparent and contains no chloroplasts, so it passes light to the cells beneath.
Below the upper epidermis lie the palisade mesophyll cells, elongated, arranged in one or more rows and filled with chloroplasts. This is where most photosynthesis takes place.
Many leaves also have few or no stomata on the upper surface, and when they do, it is usually on a leaf that floats and receives light from above.
bullets: Cuticle: reduces uncontrolled water loss.
Upper epidermis: transparent, no chloroplasts.
Palisade mesophyll: chloroplast-packed, main photosynthesis tissue.
content.takeaway: Light arrives through the top; water is lost through the bottom.

check.question: Which layer blocks most uncontrolled water loss?
check.why: The cuticle is a waterproof layer over the epidermis.

content.heading: The middle: light and gas exchange
paragraphs: Between the palisade and the lower epidermis is the spongy mesophyll: loosely arranged parenchyma cells with large intercellular air spaces. Those spaces connect with the stomata below, so carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour diffuse quickly to and from the cells.

Veins run through the mesophyll, packed into vascular bundles. In most dicot leaves, xylem lies towards the upper side of the midrib and phloem towards the lower side. Xylem brings the water that photosynthesis needs; phloem carries the sugars away.
The veins also serve as the leaf's skeleton. The central midrib branches into smaller veins, giving the leaf its shape and plumbing the mesophyll.
bullets: Spongy mesophyll: loose with large air spaces.
Vein bundles: xylem above, phloem below.
Veins support the leaf and carry water in, food out.
content.takeaway: The middle of the leaf breathes and ships its cargo.

check.question: The air spaces in the spongy mesophyll mainly speed up
check.why: Large air spaces shorten the path for gas diffusion.

content.heading: The lower surface and veins
paragraphs: The lower epidermis carries the stomata. Each stoma is a pore bordered by two guard cells. When the guard cells take up water they swell and bend outwards, opening the pore; when they lose water they shrink and close it. This controls water loss and gas exchange together.

Most dicot leaves keep most stomata on the lower surface because the upper surface is exposed to light and heat; placing the stomata there would waste water. Shade leaves and the leaves of floating plants often have stomata on both surfaces.
In a T.S., stomata and guard cells are the signature of the lower epidermis. The midrib carries the main vein and gives the leaf its central ridge.
bullets: Most stomata sit on the lower side of the leaf.
Guard cells open and close the pore by changing turgor.
Midrib: carries the main vein and supports the leaf.
content.takeaway: Stomata are the leaf's adjustable windows.

check.question: Guard cells open a stoma when they
check.why: Guard cells swell as they take up water, bending apart to open the pore.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Read a leaf T.S. from the top: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade, spongy mesophyll, lower epidermis with stomata. If stomata appear on the upper side, the leaf is usually floating.

lessons.title: Supporting Tissues in Plants
lessons.objective: Identify collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem fibres and describe their distribution in roots, stems and leaves.

content.heading: Support without bones
paragraphs: A plant holds itself up with living, corner-thickened cells and dead, lignified ones. Where each kind sits tells you what the plant is doing with its support.

content.heading: The four supporting tissues
paragraphs: Collenchyma is living at maturity. Its cell walls are unevenly thickened, often at the corners, with cellulose and pectin. It hugs young stems, petioles and leaf stalks, giving flexible support that can bend.

Sclerenchyma is dead at maturity. Its walls are thickened with lignin. Fibres are long and spindle-shaped and give tensile strength to stems and leaves; sclereids are short and brittle and make hard shells, stone fruit and the grit in a pear gritty.

Xylem vessels and tracheids are dead at maturity and lignified, so they carry water and hold the stem rigid. Phloem fibres, lying within the phloem patches, are also lignified and are used where toughness is needed; they are also called bast fibres.
bullets: Collenchyma: living, corner-thickened, cellulose and pectin.
Sclerenchyma: dead, walls thickened with lignin.
Xylem and phloem fibres: lignified and rigid.
content.takeaway: Living cells bend; lignified cells hold.

check.question: Which supporting tissue is living at maturity?
check.why: Collenchyma is the living supporting tissue with cellulose/pectin corner thickening.

content.heading: Where the support sits
paragraphs: In a young stem, collenchyma lies directly under the epidermis. Sclerenchyma fibres cap the vascular bundles, especially in flax, jute and similar crop plants, and xylem lies inside. In leaves, the midrib and the main veins carry bundles of both tissues.
In roots, xylem occupies the centre because a root pushes through soil more than it lifts a canopy. There is usually little sclerenchyma because roots are rarely in tension.
Examples for exams: fibre caps in the stem are sclerenchyma; collenchyma in celery stalks snaps first when bent; xylem supports the woody stem by way of its vessels and fibres.
bullets: Stem: collenchyma under epidermis, sclerenchyma caps the bundles.
Root: xylem at the centre.
Leaf: support runs in the midrib and main veins.
content.takeaway: Where the load is, the fibres are.

check.question: In a young stem, collenchyma is found
check.why: Collenchyma hugs the stem directly beneath the epidermis.

content.heading: How to read the section
paragraphs: Exam questions turn support into descriptions: uneven thickening and living cells give collenchyma; dead, lignified cells give sclerenchyma or xylem; dead cells in the phloem patches are the phloem fibres.

Then locate each tissue. Collenchyma beneath the epidermis in young stems is a young-plant clue; sclerenchyma in bast fibres is a flax or jute clue; xylem at the centre is a root clue; xylem inside and phloem outside in scattered patches is a monocot stem.
So the full answer chains together: the identity of the tissue, its wall chemistry, and its location in the organ.
bullets: Wall chemistry names the tissue: cellulose vs lignin.
Location: under epidermis, bundle caps, centre or veins.
Chain identity plus wall chemistry plus location.
content.takeaway: Name the tissue, state its wall, then say where it sits.

check.question: Cells described as dead at maturity with walls thickened by lignin are
check.why: Both sclerenchyma and xylem are lignified and dead at maturity.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If the cell is living with corner thickening, it is collenchyma; if it is dead and lignified it is sclerenchyma or xylem; if the fibres lie among phloem patches, they are phloem fibres.

steps.result: Flexible support under tension.

hints: Their walls are thickened with lignin.

lessons.title: Mammalian Internal Organs
lessons.objective: Examine the arrangement of the mammalian internal organs and describe the appearance and position of the digestive, reproductive and excretory organs.

content.heading: Inside the mammal
paragraphs: The diaphragm splits the trunk into thorax above and abdomen below. Once you know which systems live in which cavity, the organ map stops being a guessing game.

content.heading: The two body cavities
paragraphs: The thoracic cavity holds the lungs on either side, the heart between them, slightly to the left, and the thymus above. They are protected by the ribcage.

Below the diaphragm, the abdominal cavity holds the stomach high on the left, J-shaped; the liver and its gall bladder under the diaphragm on the right; the spleen behind the stomach; the pancreas behind the stomach; the kidneys on the posterior abdominal wall; and the intestines filling the lower cavity. The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm to reach the stomach.
The organs themselves are covered by membrane: pleura around the lungs and pericardium around the heart. In the abdomen, the visceral and parietal peritoneum wrap and suspend the gut organs.
bullets: Thorax: lungs and heart.
Abdomen: liver, stomach, pancreas, spleen.
Kidneys: posterior abdominal wall (retroperitoneal).
content.takeaway: Thorax is lung and heart territory; abdomen is the workshop.

check.question: Which organ sits mostly on the right side under the diaphragm?
check.why: The liver is the largest organ (after skin) and tucks under the diaphragm on the right.

content.heading: The digestive layout
paragraphs: Follow the food: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, ascending, transverse and descending colon, finally the rectum and anus.

Accessory organs feed the tract. The salivary glands open into the mouth; the liver produces bile which is stored in and released from the gall bladder; the pancreas makes digestive enzymes and insulin. Bile and pancreatic juice enter at the duodenum, the first section of the small intestine.

The small intestine is long and folded to maximise surface area for digestion and absorption. The large intestine reabsorbs water and houses bacteria; its appendix (vermiform) dangles from the caecum.
bullets: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → ileum → colon.
Liver makes bile; gall bladder stores it.
Pancreas: enzymes and hormones.
content.takeaway: The duodenum is where liver and pancreas meet the meal.

check.question: Bile is produced in the liver and stored in the
check.why: Bile flows to the gall bladder to be concentrated and stored.

content.heading: Excretory and reproductive position
paragraphs: The urinary system lives mostly in the abdomen. The kidneys are bean-shaped, about eleven centimetres long, on the posterior abdominal wall; the right kidney sits slightly lower because of the liver. Each kidney sends urine into a ureter that descends to the bladder; the urethra expels urine from the bladder.

In the male, the testes sit in the scrotum below the abdomen, keeping them a few degrees cooler than the abdominal cavity, which is essential for sperm production. Sperm travels through the epididymis and vas deferens past the prostate gland and out through the penis.

In the female, the ovaries lie on either side of the uterus in the pelvic cavity. Each ovary releases ova into a Fallopian tube, which carries them to the uterus, pear-shaped and midline, lying between the bladder and the rectum, and opening below into the vagina.
bullets: Kidneys: posterior wall, right lower than left.
Male: testes in the scrotum.
Female: ovaries, Fallopian tubes, uterus, vagina.
content.takeaway: Where an organ sits is the clue to what it does.

check.question: The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left because of the position of the
check.why: The liver occupies the right upper abdomen and pushes the kidney down.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Halve the trunk at the diaphragm. Lungs and heart are above it; liver right, spleen left, kidneys posterior, uterus midline between bladder and rectum.

lessons.title: Modes of Nutrition
lessons.objective: Compare autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition and differentiate the holozoic, parasitic, saprophytic and carnivorous-plant types.

content.heading: Modes of nutrition
paragraphs: Two green plants can sit in the same soil and get fed very differently. That difference decides what a plant can and cannot survive on.

content.heading: Autotrophs make their own food; heterotrophs take it
paragraphs: A maize plant growing in a cassava farm in Ogun State feeds without eating anything. The same species planted in the same field, but in a dim, shaded spot, grows slowly and pale. The sunlight is mature feed for the first and missing feed for the second.

Autotrophs make their own organic food from simple inorganic ingredients, mainly carbon (IV) oxide and water, using energy from sunlight. Plants and algae are the examples JAMB wants, and the food they make is called organic.

Heterotrophs cannot make their own food and must absorb or ingest ready-made organic food from a living or dead source. Man, sheep, Rhizopus, mushroom and tapeworm are heterotrophs; they need a food source that is already organic.
bullets: Autotrophs make their own organic food from simple inorganic ingredients.
Heterotrophs take in ready-made organic food.
Plants and algae are autotrophs; animals and fungi are heterotrophs.
content.takeaway: Autotrophs make food; heterotrophs take it.

check.question: An organism that makes its own food from carbon (IV) oxide and water is
check.why: Making food from simple inorganic ingredients defines an autotroph.

content.heading: Four heterotrophic patterns
paragraphs: A child eats eba, then the food is taken into the body and digested. A tapeworm inside the same child has no such step. Both feed heterotrophically, but the way each one gets its food is different.

Holozoic feeders ingest solid food into the body and digest it internally, for example man and sheep. Parasites absorb or ingest food from a living host while harming it, for example tapeworm, roundworm and Loranthus.
Saprophytes absorb food dissolved from dead matter, for example Rhizopus and mushroom. Carnivorous plants trap and digest insects, for example sundew and bladderwort.
bullets: Holozoic: ingest solid food and digest it, for example man and sheep.
Parasitic: feed on a living host without killing it, for example tapeworm, roundworm and Loranthus.
Saprophytic: absorb food released from dead matter, for example Rhizopus and mushroom.
Carnivorous plants trap and digest insects, for example sundew and bladderwort.
content.takeaway: Holozoic ingests, parasitic uses a host, saprophytes use dead matter.

check.question: Rhizopus that feeds on bread is an example of
check.why: Rhizopus secretes enzymes outside the body and absorbs food from dead bread.

content.heading: Nutrition is about sources, not the eater alone
paragraphs: A sundew in a marsh catches a fly and digests it. A tree beside it makes food all day. Both are plants; the diet differs in source, not in organ.

So judge by where the nutrition comes from: a holozoic eater ingests, a parasite uses a living host, a saprophyte uses dead matter, a carnivorous plant supplements minerals. Plants are usually autotrophs, but they may also be saprophytes or parasites, while no animal is an autotroph.
Exam hint: if the question asks about a plant that traps insects, it is not a carnivorous plant by anatomy; it is supplementing short minerals from insects while keeping its photosynthesis.
bullets: Saprophytes are mainly fungi; carnivorous plants are green plants that supplement minerals.
Parasites derive food from a living host and usually harm it.
Autotrophs manufacture food; heterotrophs absorb or ingest it.
content.takeaway: Name where the food comes from, not merely who eats.

check.question: A plant that makes its own food and also traps insects is both
check.why: Sundew and bladderwort photosynthesise and supplement minerals from insects.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Look for the source word: ingest means holozoic, host means parasitic, dead means saprophytic, trap means carnivorous.

content.problem: Classify each feeding pattern: tapeworm in humans, mushroom on decaying wood, sundew leaves, and a yam plant.

steps.reason: Tapeworm lives and feeds inside a human intestine.
steps.result: Parasitic.
steps.predictPrompt: Which pattern is shown by mushroom on decaying wood?

steps.reason: Mushroom secretes enzymes onto rotten wood and absorbs the products.
steps.result: Saprophytic.

steps.reason: Sundew traps insects on sticky leaves.
steps.result: Carnivorous plant (also an autotroph).

steps.reason: Yam stores starch made in leaves from carbon (IV) oxide and water.
steps.result: Autotrophic.

content.question: Explain why sundew is both an autotroph and a carnivorous plant.
hints: Its leaves contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise.
Insects supply the mineral salts the soil lacks.
Nutrition type describes the source of food, not one label per organism.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Mineral Requirements
lessons.objective: Differentiate the light and dark reactions of photosynthesis, show the necessity of light, carbon (IV) oxide and chlorophyll, and identify macro- and micronutrients with their deficiency symptoms.

content.heading: Photosynthesis and mineral requirements
paragraphs: A leaf in a covered jar can still be green but stop making starch. The leaf is alive; the missing ingredient is what the question is really testing.

content.heading: Light reactions and dark reactions
paragraphs: Place a leaf in light that has been filtered through a screen, and the part that forms starch is the part the light hit. Leaves kept in the dark do not form starch at all.

In the light reaction, chlorophyll absorbs light energy. The energy splits water (photolysis) into hydrogen and oxygen, and oxygen is released. The energy is trapped in carriers for the dark reactions.

In the dark reaction, glucose is manufactured from carbon (IV) oxide using the energy supplied by the light reaction. It does not need light, hence the name; the two reactions are linked by the energy carriers made in the light reaction.
bullets: Light reactions: need light, split water, release oxygen, make energy carriers.
Dark reactions: no light needed, fix carbon (IV) oxide into glucose.
Starch in a leaf is evidence that photosynthesis has occurred.
content.takeaway: Light splits water; the dark reactions fix carbon.

check.question: Oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from the splitting of
check.why: Photolysis splits water and oxygen is released in the light reaction.

content.heading: Why no light, no carbon (IV) oxide, no chlorophyll means no starch
paragraphs: A variegated leaf with white patches and a green part produces starch only in the green part. A leaf covered so that light cannot reach it produces no starch at all. A destarched leaf enclosed in carbon (IV) oxide-free air produces no starch either.
Light delivers the energy, carbon (IV) oxide supplies the carbon skeleton of glucose, and chlorophyll captures the energy. All three are necessary; remove any one and starch formation stops.

The iodine test confirms starch: the leaf is boiled, treated with alcohol and iodine; a blue-black colour shows starch. A leaf that was kept in the dark next to a leaf in light is the control; the part that stays brown has no starch.
bullets: Light, carbon (IV) oxide and chlorophyll are all needed for photosynthesis.
Variegated leaf test: only the green part makes starch.
Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch.
content.takeaway: No light, no carbon (IV) oxide or no chlorophyll means no photosynthesis.

check.question: In the experiment to show that light is needed for photosynthesis, what is done to the leaf?
check.why: Light must be excluded from one part to test its necessity.

content.heading: Chemosynthesis and mineral requirements
paragraphs: Some bacteria in the soil do not need sunlight at all. They get their energy from oxidised chemicals, especially sulphur and iron compounds. That is chemosynthesis, distinct from photosynthesis because the energy source is chemical rather than light.

Plants need mineral salts for growth. The macronutrients required in large quantities are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK). Nitrogen is needed for proteins and chlorophyll; deficiency shows yellow older leaves, called chlorosis. Phosphorus is needed for roots and seeds; deficiency gives stunted growth and purplish leaves. Potassium controls stomatal opening and enzyme activation; deficiency causes mottled leaves and weak stems.

Micronutrients, needed in small amounts, include iron, magnesium, calcium, zinc and boron. Magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis because magnesium is the centre of the chlorophyll molecule. Iron deficiency also causes chlorosis in young leaves.
bullets: Chemosynthesis: energy from chemical oxidation, used by bacteria.
Macronutrients: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium.
Micronutrients: iron, magnesium, calcium, zinc, boron.
Nitrogen, iron, magnesium deficiency: chlorosis (yellow leaves).
content.takeaway: Photosynthesis uses light; chemosynthesis uses chemicals and NPK feed the plant.

check.question: Yellowing of older leaves indicates deficiency of
check.why: Nitrogen deficiency shows chlorosis in older leaves first.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Photosynthesis needs light; chemosynthesis does not. Macronutrients are NPK; micronutrients are trace. Chlorosis signals nitrogen, iron or magnesium deficiency.

content.problem: Suggest a remedy: a young orange tree shows pale green veins but dark green between them, and the older leaves are also pale.

steps.reason: Chlorosis shows depletion of a green-making nutrient.
steps.result: Chlorosis, characteristic of magnesium deficiency.
steps.predictPrompt: What nutrient is needed for chlorophyll?

steps.reason: Magnesium is the centre of the chlorophyll molecule.
steps.result: Established as magnesium deficiency.

steps.reason: Mineral salts must be replaced in soil fertiliser.
steps.result: Apply a magnesium-containing fertiliser (e.g. Epsom salts).

content.question: Explain why a variegated-leaf experiment proves chlorophyll is necessary for photosynthesis.
hints: The white parts lack chlorophyll.
They receive light and carbon (IV) oxide but cannot trap energy.
Starch is found only in the green parts after iodine testing.

lessons.title: Classes of Food and Balanced Diet
lessons.objective: Identify the six classes of food, indicate their sources and importance, perform food tests, and relate each class to its deficiency disease.

content.heading: Classes of food and balanced diet
paragraphs: Two children eat lunch in the same school in Lagos: one eats rice, beans and fish; the other eats only puff-puff. By the end of term, the second child is often tired and pale. The difference is the mix of food classes.

content.heading: The six classes and where they come from
paragraphs: Carbohydrates supply energy and are found in yam, rice, eba, maize, bread and plantain. Proteins build and repair tissues; fish, meat, eggs, beans and milk are the main sources. Fats and oils store energy, insulate the body and protect organs; palm oil, groundnut oil, margarine and butter are the sources.

Mineral salts build bones and teeth, regulate body fluids and help enzymes work; iron comes from leafy vegetables, fish and blood-rich meats, while calcium comes from milk, fish bones and leafy greens. Water regulates body temperature, dissolves wastes and transports nutrients.
Vitamins regulate body processes; vitamin A prevents night blindness, vitamins B and C prevent beriberi and scurvy, vitamin D prevents rickets.
bullets: Carbohydrates: energy (yam, rice, maize, bread).
Proteins: growth and repair (fish, meat, eggs, beans).
Fats and oils: energy store and insulation (palm oil, groundnut oil).
Mineral salts and water: structure, transport and regulation.
Vitamins: regulate body processes (A, B, C, D).
content.takeaway: Six classes: energy, building blocks, protection and regulation.

check.question: Proteins are needed in the body for
check.why: Proteins build and repair cells and tissues.

content.heading: Food tests identify each class
paragraphs: To know what a food sample contains, use chemical tests. Iodine solution gives a blue-black colour with starch. Benedict's solution, when heated with a reducing sugar, changes from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red.
For protein, the biuret test gives a purple colour. For fats, the emulsion test gives a white emulsion when alcohol is mixed with the sample. These tests identify food types from experiment results.
Use the tests as a checklist: blue-black is starch; a colour change in Benedict's is reducing sugar; purple in biuret is protein; emulsion is fat.
bullets: Starch: blue-black with iodine.
Reducing sugar: blue to brick-red with Benedict's solution.
Protein: purple with biuret solution.
Fat: white emulsion with alcohol.
content.takeaway: Iodine for starch, Benedict's for sugar, biuret for protein, emulsion for fat.

check.question: A food sample that turns iodine solution blue-black contains
check.why: Iodine gives a blue-black colour in the presence of starch.

content.heading: Balanced diet and deficiency diseases
paragraphs: A balanced diet supplies the right amount of each class in proportions the body needs. A school lunch of rice (carbohydrates), beans (protein), palm oil (fats), vegetable (vitamins and minerals) and water is balanced; puff-puff and fanta alone is not.

When one class falls short, a deficiency disease appears. Scurvy is caused by lack of vitamin C and shows bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Rickets is caused by lack of vitamin D and calcium and shows bow legs and soft bones in children. Kwashiorkor is caused by lack of protein and shows a swollen belly, oedema and listlessness.

Marasmus is a more severe protein-energy malnutrition showing a 'skin and bones' appearance. Night blindness shows lack of vitamin A; beriberi shows lack of vitamin B. Recognising each pattern links the food class to the disease.
bullets: Balanced diet: all six classes in recommended proportions.
Scurvy: vitamin C deficiency.
Rickets: vitamin D and calcium deficiency.
Kwashiorkor and marasmus: protein deficiency.
Night blindness: vitamin A deficiency.
content.takeaway: A balanced diet has all six classes; each deficiency has a name.

check.question: A child with a swollen belly, oedema and flaky skin is likely suffering from
check.why: Kwashiorkor is protein-energy malnutrition with oedema.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Match the deficiency to the missing class: vitamin C is scurvy, vitamin D/calcium is rickets, protein is kwashiorkor or marasmus.

content.problem: An experiment: a food extract turns iodine blue-black, a second turns Benedict's solution brick-red, and a third gives a purple colour with biuret. Identify each food type.

steps.reason: Blue-black indicates starch.
steps.result: Starch.
steps.predictPrompt: What test confirms protein?

steps.reason: Blue to brick-red indicates a reducing sugar.
steps.result: Reducing sugar (glucose, fructose).

steps.reason: Purple indicates protein.
steps.result: Protein.

content.question: Why is a meal of yam, pepper soup and water not balanced? Name what is missing.
hints: Yam supplies carbohydrates only.
Pepper soup has vitamins but very little protein.
Protein for growth and repair is missing.

lessons.title: Mammalian Teeth and Alimentary Canal
lessons.objective: Describe the structure of a typical mammalian tooth, differentiate the types and relate them to their functions, compare dental formulae, and relate the alimentary canal and its accessory organs to their functions.

content.heading: Mammalian teeth and alimentary canal
paragraphs: A goat grazing tough grass and a dog tearing meat both have molars, but the rest of the mouth differs sharply. The mouth shows what the animal eats.

content.heading: Structure of a tooth
paragraphs: A tooth has a crown above the gum and a root below. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body, which resists acids and wear. The root is held in a socket by cement and anchored by gum and ligaments.

Beneath the enamel is dentine, a hard but sensitive layer. The pulp cavity at the centre holds nerves and blood vessels. Mammalian teeth are heterodont, meaning they differ in shape within the same mouth.
Each tooth is adapted by shape to a job: incisors are chisel-shaped for cutting, canines are pointed for tearing, premolars and molars are flat-topped for grinding.
bullets: Crown (enamel) resists wear; root anchors the tooth.
Dentine is sensitive; pulp carries nerves and vessels.
Heterodont: different shapes, different jobs.
content.takeaway: Enamel resists, dentine senses, and shape decides the job.

check.question: The hardest substance in the body, covering the tooth crown, is
check.why: Enamel is the hardest tissue and protects the crown.

content.heading: Tooth types and dental formulae
paragraphs: Man has incisors for biting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding. Dogs have large canines and shearing carnassial teeth for meat. In herbivores like sheep, the upper incisors are replaced by a horny dental pad, and the cheek teeth are high-crowned for grinding grass.

A dental formula lists, in order, incisors, canines, premolars and molars in the upper and lower jaw. Man: 2/2, 1/1, 2/2, 3/3 = 32 teeth. Dog: 3/3, 1/1, 4/4, 2/3 = 42 teeth. Sheep: 0/3, 0/1, 3/3, 3/3 = 32 teeth.
The number and pattern show diet: many grinders mean herbivory, strong canines mean carnivory, and an even mix means omnivory.
bullets: Incisors bite, canines tear, cheek teeth grind.
Man has 32 teeth; dog 42; sheep 32 with a dental pad.
Dental formula: incisors/canines/premolars/molars, upper over lower.
content.takeaway: Count the teeth and you know the diet.

check.question: Which dental feature is typical of a grass-eating herbivore?
options: A horny dental pad instead of upper incisors
check.why: Sheep and goats have a dental pad in place of upper incisors.

content.heading: The alimentary canal and its accessory organs
paragraphs: Food moves through the canal in steps, each part doing a job. The salivary glands moisten food and contain amylase. The oesophagus pushes food with peristalsis, the rhythmic muscular contraction. The stomach churns the food and secretes hydrochloric acid and protease.

In the small intestine, the food is completed: bile from the liver emulsifies fats, pancreatic juice from the pancreas supplies amylase, trypsin and lipase, and the succus entericus completes digestion. The duodenum is where bile and pancreatic juice enter.

Absorption happens mainly in the ileum, whose villi multiply the surface area. The nutrition process runs ingestion, digestion, absorption and assimilation, with assimilation building the absorbed food into the body's tissues. In the large intestine water is reabsorbed, and the rectum stores faeces until egestion.
bullets: Mouth → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach → duodenum → ileum → colon.
Bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice carries amylase, trypsin and lipase.
Villi increase the surface for absorption; the colon reabsorbs water.
content.takeaway: The gut moves, churns, digests, absorbs and then expels.

check.question: Peristalsis is the movement of food through the oesophagus by
check.why: Waves of muscular contraction push food along the oesophagus.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Dental formula always lists I/C/P/M. Bile emulsifies but does not digest; pancreatic juice digests all three classes.

content.problem: An animal has a dental formula 0/3, 0/1, 3/3, 3/3. What does it eat and why?

steps.reason: No upper incisors and no upper canines, but many cheek teeth.
steps.result: The animal grinds rather than bites or tears.
steps.predictPrompt: Which mammal has a dental pad like this?

steps.reason: Cheek teeth for grinding suit fibrous plant food.
steps.result: It is a herbivore, like sheep.

steps.reason: Canines would indicate meat-tearing; their absence excludes a carnivore.
steps.result: Concluded as herbivore.

content.question: Why does bile help digestion without itself digesting?
hints: Bile contains no digestive enzymes.
Bile salts emulsify large fat droplets into smaller ones.
Emulsification increases the surface area for pancreatic lipase to act on.

lessons.title: Why Transport?
lessons.objective: Relate increasing size and complexity to the need for transport, identify the materials transported and their sources, and name the media and channels used.

content.heading: Why transport?
paragraphs: A pond Amoeba and an elephant both need oxygen, but only the Amoeba can rely on diffusion through its surface. Increasing size and complexity create a transport problem.

content.heading: Why size changes the problem
paragraphs: An Amoeba in pond water is one cell, so oxygen and food reach the cytoplasm by diffusion over a very short distance. Its surface area is large compared with its volume, and no part of the cell is far from the water outside.

A maize plant or a goat is different. Most cells sit deep inside the body, far from the air and food, so diffusion alone would be too slow to supply them. The distance is too long and the demand too high.

Larger, more active organisms therefore need a transport system: a set of channels and a moving medium that carries materials quickly between organs. The system links the surfaces where materials enter or leave with the tissues that use or make them.
bullets: Small organisms: short diffusion distances and a large surface-to-volume ratio.
Large organisms: long distances and high demand.
A transport system carries materials between surfaces and tissues.
content.takeaway: Size creates distance; transport closes it.

check.question: Why does a large, active animal need a transport system?
options: Its cells are too small to absorb oxygen
Its surface has no exchange organs
Diffusion alone is too slow over long distances
It cannot make its own food
check.why: Large bodies have long diffusion distances and high demand, so bulk transport is needed.

content.heading: What the transport system carries
paragraphs: Blood does not carry one substance. It carries gases, digested food, manufactured food, excretory products, mineral salts, water and hormones, and each has a source and a destination.

Oxygen enters at the lungs and travels to every tissue, while carbon (IV) oxide travels the other way. Glucose and amino acids enter at the small intestine and reach the liver and cells; urea is made in the liver and carried to the kidneys.

Plants move sucrose and amino acids from leaves to growing parts, and water with dissolved mineral salts from roots to leaves. Hormones such as insulin travel in blood from endocrine glands to target organs, so the system also carries chemical messages.
bullets: Gases: oxygen to tissues; carbon (IV) oxide to the lungs.
Food and wastes: glucose and amino acids to cells; urea to the kidneys.
Water, mineral salts and hormones also travel in the transport medium.
content.takeaway: Transport carries raw materials, wastes and messages.

check.question: Urea is transported from the liver to the
check.why: Urea is a nitrogenous waste carried in blood to the kidneys for excretion.

content.heading: Media and channels
paragraphs: The medium is what actually carries the material. In Amoeba it is the cytoplasm; in a plant cell it is the cell sap; in an insect it is the body fluid called haemolymph; in a mammal it is blood and lymph.

The channel is the route. Mammals have blood vessels, plants have xylem and phloem, and very small organisms may have no special channel at all. A medium without a channel can still move by diffusion, but a large organism needs both.
Open systems such as those of insects pour haemolymph into body spaces, while closed systems keep blood inside vessels. The next lessons follow the mammalian and plant systems in turn.
bullets: Media: cytoplasm, cell sap, haemolymph, blood and lymph.
Channels: blood vessels in mammals; xylem and phloem in plants.
Large organisms need both a medium and a channel.
content.takeaway: A medium carries; a channel directs.

check.question: Which of these is a channel for transport in a flowering plant?
check.why: Xylem and phloem are the plant's transport channels; the other options are media.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB often asks for the source and destination of a material. Say where it is made or absorbed, what carries it, and where it is used or removed.

content.problem: A goat eats grass. Trace four materials from their source to their destination.

steps.reason: Starch in grass is digested to glucose in the small intestine.
steps.result: Absorbed into blood and carried to the liver and muscles.
steps.predictPrompt: Where is urea made?

steps.reason: The liver breaks down excess amino acids and forms urea.
steps.result: Carried by blood to the kidneys and excreted in urine.

steps.reason: Oxygen is absorbed at the lungs and bound by haemoglobin.
steps.result: Carried by blood to respiring cells.

steps.reason: The pancreas makes insulin and releases it into blood.
steps.result: Carried to the liver and muscles, where it lowers blood glucose.

content.question: Explain why an Amoeba does not need a circulatory system but a goat does.
hints: Compare surface area with volume in each organism.
Diffusion is fast only over very short distances.
A goat has a high demand for oxygen and food in cells deep inside its body.

lessons.title: The Mammalian Circulatory System
lessons.objective: Describe the mammalian heart and double circulation, compare arteries, veins and capillaries, and relate the named vessels to their functions.

content.heading: The mammalian circulatory system
paragraphs: A cyclist climbing a Lagos bridge feels her heart pound. The pump is moving oxygen faster because her muscles now demand more of it. That is the circulatory system at work.

content.heading: The heart and double circulation
paragraphs: The mammalian heart has four chambers: two thin-walled atria above and two thick-walled ventricles below. The right side receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body.

Valves between the chambers and at the exits keep blood moving one way. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must push blood around the whole body, while the right ventricle only reaches the lungs.

This is a double circulation: pulmonary through the lungs and systemic through the body. Insects have an open system instead, with haemolymph bathing the organs, while mammals keep blood in closed vessels.
bullets: Right side: body to lungs. Left side: lungs to body.
Valves prevent backflow; the left ventricle has the thickest wall.
Mammals have closed circulation; insects have an open system.
content.takeaway: Two circuits, one pump, and valves that keep blood moving forward.

check.question: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body?
check.why: The left ventricle sends blood into the aorta and around the systemic circuit.

content.heading: Arteries, veins and capillaries
paragraphs: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. They have thick, elastic muscular walls and a narrow lumen, which withstand the high pressure produced by each heartbeat. The pulmonary artery is an exception to the oxygen rule: it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

Veins carry blood back to the heart. Their walls are thinner, their lumen wider, and valves stop backflow in the low-pressure system. Capillaries are one cell thick, so gases, glucose and wastes can pass between blood and tissue fluid.
Arteries branch into arterioles, then capillaries, then venules and veins. The capillary network is where exchange happens; the great vessels are only the delivery roads.
bullets: Arteries: thick walls, narrow lumen, blood away from the heart.
Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves, blood back to the heart.
Capillaries: one-cell walls for exchange with tissue fluid.
content.takeaway: Arteries deliver, veins return, capillaries exchange.

check.question: Which blood vessel has valves along its length to prevent backflow?
check.why: Veins carry blood at low pressure and use valves to keep it moving toward the heart.

content.heading: Named vessels and what they carry
paragraphs: Some vessels are named for the organ they serve. The aorta leaves the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the body. The pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle with deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

The hepatic portal vein is unusual. It carries blood from the small intestine and other digestive organs to the liver, so digested food is processed before entering the general circulation. It is not the hepatic vein, which drains the liver into the vena cava.

The renal artery takes oxygenated blood to the kidney, and the renal vein carries filtered, deoxygenated blood away. The hepatic portal vein therefore has two capillary beds in series, while the renal vessels serve one organ.
bullets: Aorta: left ventricle to body; pulmonary artery: right ventricle to lungs.
Pulmonary vein: lungs to left atrium; renal artery and vein: kidney.
Hepatic portal vein: intestine to liver, carrying digested food.
content.takeaway: Read the name: pulmonary means lungs, hepatic means liver, renal means kidney.

check.question: Which vessel carries digested food from the intestine to the liver?
check.why: The hepatic portal vein links the intestinal capillaries to the liver capillaries.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Do not judge a vessel by its oxygen content alone. The pulmonary artery is deoxygenated and the pulmonary vein oxygenated; the hepatic portal vein carries food-rich blood.

content.problem: Trace a red blood cell from the right atrium to the aorta. Name the chambers, valves and vessels in order.

steps.reason: Blood flows from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve.
steps.result: Right ventricle.
steps.predictPrompt: Where does the right ventricle send blood?

steps.reason: The right ventricle contracts and pushes blood into the pulmonary artery.
steps.result: Lungs, where the blood becomes oxygenated.

steps.reason: Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary vein.
steps.result: Left atrium.

steps.reason: Blood passes through the bicuspid valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta.
steps.result: Aorta and the systemic circulation.

content.question: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle.
hints: Compare the distance blood travels in the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
The systemic circuit has greater resistance to flow.
A thicker wall can produce a higher pressure.

lessons.title: Blood and Lymph
lessons.objective: State the composition and functions of blood and lymph, and explain how tissue fluid, plasma, blood cells and platelets carry out transport and defence.

content.heading: Blood and lymph
paragraphs: A blood donation session in Abuja separates whole blood into plasma, cells and platelets. Each part has a different job in transport and defence, and lymph is the second fluid.

content.heading: Plasma: the liquid cargo
paragraphs: Plasma is about 55% of blood volume and is mostly water, with dissolved proteins, mineral salts, glucose, amino acids, hormones, urea and carbon (IV) oxide. It is the medium that carries blood cells and dissolved materials around the body.
The plasma proteins have separate jobs. Fibrinogen is needed for clotting; albumin helps hold water in the blood and keeps osmotic pressure steady; globulins include antibodies that fight infection.
Plasma also distributes heat from active organs and buffers small changes in pH. Serum is plasma after clotting proteins have been removed, which is why serum is used in some tests.
bullets: Plasma is mostly water and carries dissolved food, wastes and hormones.
Fibrinogen clots, albumin holds water, globulins include antibodies.
Plasma distributes heat and buffers pH; serum is plasma without clotting proteins.
content.takeaway: Plasma is the liquid road; its proteins clot, balance water and fight infection.

check.question: Which plasma protein is needed for blood clotting?
check.why: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin threads during clotting.

content.heading: Red cells, white cells and platelets
paragraphs: Red blood cells are biconcave discs without a nucleus in mammals. They are packed with haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues; their shape gives a large surface area and their flexibility lets them squeeze through capillaries.

White blood cells defend the body. Phagocytes engulf bacteria and debris, while lymphocytes make antibodies and coordinate immune responses. They are fewer than red cells but can leave the blood to reach an infection.
Platelets are cell fragments that start clotting when a vessel is damaged. They clump at the break and help convert fibrinogen into fibrin threads, which trap blood cells and form a plug.
bullets: Red cells: haemoglobin, biconcave shape, about 120 days in circulation.
White cells: phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies.
Platelets: cell fragments that start clot formation.
content.takeaway: Red cells carry oxygen, white cells defend, platelets seal leaks.

check.question: Which blood component produces antibodies?
check.why: Lymphocytes are white blood cells that produce antibodies against specific antigens.

content.heading: Lymph and tissue fluid
paragraphs: Blood pressure at the arterial end of a capillary pushes water and small solutes into the spaces between cells. This fluid is tissue fluid; it supplies cells and collects their wastes, but it has no red cells or platelets.

Most tissue fluid returns to the venous end of the capillary. The rest enters blind-ended lymph capillaries and becomes lymph, which passes through lymph nodes and is returned to the blood through veins near the neck.

Lymph carries lymphocytes and absorbed fats from the villi, and its valves and body movements keep it moving. If lymph vessels are blocked, tissue fluid accumulates and causes oedema, as in filariasis.
bullets: Tissue fluid bathes cells and exchanges materials with them.
Lymph returns excess tissue fluid via lymph nodes and veins.
Lymph carries lymphocytes and absorbed fats; blockage causes oedema.
content.takeaway: Tissue fluid bathes cells; lymph returns the excess.

check.question: Lymph differs from blood because lymph lacks
check.why: Red cells and platelets stay in capillaries, so lymph is clear and carries lymphocytes.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Blood has red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma; lymph has lymphocytes but no red cells. Tissue fluid is the fluid between cells.

content.problem: A patient has swollen legs and a blocked lymph vessel. Explain the swelling and trace the normal return of tissue fluid.

steps.reason: The swelling is tissue fluid that has not returned to the blood.
steps.result: Tissue fluid accumulation, called oedema.
steps.predictPrompt: What vessel normally drains tissue fluid?

steps.reason: A blocked lymph vessel raises the pressure in the lymph capillaries.
steps.result: Less tissue fluid can drain away, so it collects in the tissues.

steps.reason: Lymph capillaries join larger lymph vessels and pass through lymph nodes.
steps.result: Lymph returns to the blood through veins near the neck.

content.question: Explain why lymph normally contains lymphocytes but no red blood cells.
hints: Lymph begins as tissue fluid forced out of blood capillaries.
Red cells are too large to pass through the capillary wall.
Lymphocytes can leave capillaries and enter the lymph.

lessons.title: Plant Transport
lessons.objective: Relate xylem and phloem structure to function, explain translocation, and compare transpiration pull, root pressure and active transport.

content.heading: Plant transport
paragraphs: A cassava plant wilts at midday and recovers at night. Water is moving through it all the time, even when the leaves look still.

content.heading: Xylem: water and mineral salts upward
paragraphs: Root hairs increase the surface for absorbing water. Water enters by osmosis, moves across the root and up the xylem, which is made of dead, hollow cells with lignified walls. The walls stop the tubes collapsing under tension, and xylem and phloem run through roots, stems and leaves as vascular bundles.

Water travels as a continuous column from root to leaf. It is pulled upward mainly by transpiration, the loss of water vapour through stomata, and helped by cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to the xylem walls.

Mineral salts are not simply dragged along. They are absorbed by active transport and then carried in the xylem stream to the leaves, where they are used to make proteins, chlorophyll and other compounds.
bullets: Xylem: dead, hollow, lignified cells that carry water upward.
Root hairs absorb water by osmosis; minerals enter by active transport.
Cohesion and adhesion keep the water column unbroken.
content.takeaway: Xylem is a one-way water pipeline from root to leaf.

check.question: Which tissue carries water and mineral salts from roots to leaves?
check.why: Xylem vessels and tracheids form the water-conducting pipeline of the plant.

content.heading: Phloem: food in both directions
paragraphs: Phloem carries the products of photosynthesis. Sieve tubes are living cells with perforated end walls, and each has a companion cell that supplies energy and controls loading.

Sucrose and amino acids move from a source, such as a mature leaf, to a sink, such as a growing shoot, root, fruit or storage organ. This movement is called translocation, and it can go upward or downward because the source and sink change with the season.

Loading sucrose into the phloem draws water in by osmosis, raising pressure that pushes sap toward the sink. The process uses energy from respiration, so phloem transport is active, unlike the passive pull in xylem.
bullets: Phloem: living sieve tubes with companion cells.
Translocation moves sugars and amino acids from source to sink.
Loading uses energy and pressure, so phloem transport is active.
content.takeaway: Phloem moves food from source to sink, in either direction.

check.question: The movement of sugars through phloem is called
check.why: Translocation is the transport of dissolved food through phloem from source to sink.

content.heading: Transpiration pull, root pressure and active transport
paragraphs: Transpiration pull is the main upward force in tall plants. Evaporation from the leaf lowers pressure in the xylem, and the continuous water column is pulled upward; cohesion and adhesion keep the column unbroken.

Root pressure pushes water up from below. It develops when minerals accumulate in the root and water follows by osmosis, and it is strongest at night when transpiration is low; it can cause guttation, droplets at leaf tips.

Active transport moves mineral ions against their concentration gradient using energy from respiration. Diffusion and osmosis also move materials over short distances, while bulk flow in xylem and phloem moves them over long distances.
bullets: Transpiration pull: passive upward pull driven by evaporation.
Root pressure: osmotic push, strongest at night; can cause guttation.
Active transport: uses energy to move mineral ions against a gradient.
content.takeaway: Transpiration pulls, root pressure pushes, active transport pumps.

check.question: Which mechanism mainly explains water rising in a tall tree on a hot day?
check.why: Rapid evaporation from the leaves creates the tension that pulls the water column upward.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Xylem is dead and carries water upward; phloem is living and carries food both ways. Transpiration pull is passive; active transport needs energy.

content.problem: A gardener removes a ring of bark from a young tree. Predict what happens above and below the ring.

steps.reason: The bark contains the phloem, which lies outside the xylem.
steps.result: Phloem transport is interrupted.
steps.predictPrompt: Which tissue remains able to carry water?

steps.reason: Sugars made in the leaves cannot pass down through the removed phloem.
steps.result: Sugars accumulate above the ring and the bark may swell.

steps.reason: The roots receive no sugars from the leaves.
steps.result: Root growth and respiration decline.

steps.reason: The root system starves while the shoot keeps photosynthesising.
steps.result: The tree may eventually die.

hints: Transpiration can remove water faster than roots absorb it.
Water loss lowers the turgor pressure that keeps leaves firm.
Wilting reduces water loss and can reverse when transpiration slows.

lessons.title: Diffusion, Osmosis and Water Relations
lessons.objective: Describe diffusion and osmosis, and explain plasmolysis and turgidity as the responses of plant cells to water movement.

content.heading: Diffusion, osmosis and water relations
paragraphs: A slice of fresh okra left in salt water goes limp within minutes. Water has crossed a membrane, and the direction of movement is the whole story.

content.heading: Diffusion: movement down a gradient
paragraphs: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It is passive, so it uses the random motion of particles rather than energy from respiration.

Oxygen diffuses from the air in the lungs into blood, and from blood into respiring cells. Carbon (IV) oxide diffuses the other way. In a leaf, carbon (IV) oxide enters through stomata and oxygen leaves.

The rate depends on the concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance. Small, thin surfaces with a steep gradient speed diffusion up; that is why alveoli and root hairs are finely branched and thin.
bullets: Diffusion: particles move from high to low concentration.
It is passive and depends on random particle motion.
Steep gradients, large surfaces and short distances speed it up.
content.takeaway: Diffusion is passive movement from high to low concentration.

check.question: Diffusion is described as passive because it
options: Depends on the random movement of particles
check.why: Diffusion needs no metabolic energy; particles spread by their own random motion.

content.heading: Osmosis: water across a membrane
paragraphs: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. The dilute solution has more water molecules, so water moves toward the side with less water and more solute.
An animal cell placed in distilled water gains water and may burst; in strong salt solution it loses water and shrinks. A plant cell behaves differently because its cell wall resists expansion.
Root hairs use osmosis to absorb soil water, and water moves from cell to cell across the root. Osmosis is passive, but it depends on a water potential gradient and a membrane the water can cross.
bullets: Osmosis: water moves through a partially permeable membrane.
Water moves from dilute (high water) to concentrated (low water).
Animal cells may burst or shrink; plant cell walls resist expansion.
content.takeaway: Osmosis is water movement toward the more concentrated solution.

check.question: Water moves by osmosis from
options: A concentrated solution to a dilute solution
A dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
A region of low water potential to high water potential
Any cell to any other cell
check.why: Water moves down its own gradient, from the dilute side to the more concentrated side.

content.heading: Plasmolysis and turgidity
paragraphs: When a plant cell is in pure water, water enters its vacuole by osmosis. The vacuole swells, pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall and the cell becomes turgid; turgor pressure keeps herbaceous plants upright.

In a concentrated salt or sugar solution, water leaves the vacuole. The protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall, and the cell is plasmolysed. The plant tissue becomes limp, which is why salted vegetables lose their crispness.

Plasmolysis is reversible if the cell is returned to water before the protoplast is badly damaged. Turgidity and plasmolysis explain wilting, food preservation with salt or sugar, and why fresh vegetables crisp up in cold water.
bullets: Turgid: water enters, vacuole swells, cell is firm.
Plasmolysed: water leaves, protoplast pulls away from the wall.
Turgidity supports plants; plasmolysis makes tissue limp.
content.takeaway: Turgid cells are firm; plasmolysed cells are limp.

check.question: A plant cell placed in concentrated salt solution will
options: Burst because it has no cell wall
Take in salt and become flaccid
check.why: The external solution is more concentrated, so water leaves the vacuole and the protoplast shrinks.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Diffusion moves any particles; osmosis moves only water through a membrane. Plasmolysis is the plant-cell result of water loss; turgidity is the result of water gain.

content.problem: Three potato strips are placed in distilled water, a dilute salt solution and a concentrated salt solution. Predict their firmness.

steps.reason: The cell sap is more concentrated than the surrounding water.
steps.result: Water enters by osmosis; the strip becomes turgid and firm.
steps.predictPrompt: What happens in the concentrated salt solution?

steps.reason: The gradient is small, so there is little net water movement.
steps.result: The strip stays firm, with little change in mass.

steps.reason: The external solution is more concentrated than the cell sap.
steps.result: Water leaves the cells; the strip becomes limp and plasmolysed.
